title: Gestational diabetes (ADA, NICE and WHO)
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
summary: Exclude overt diabetes early, then diagnose GDM at 24 to 28 weeks with the one-step 75 g OGTT (WHO 2013 and IADPSG, preferred by ADA), a two-step test, or NICE risk-based testing. Treat with nutrition, activity and glucose monitoring; add insulin (ADA first line) or metformin (NICE first drug) if targets are missed, and retest after birth.

sections.title: Screening and early pregnancy
items: ADA 2026: before 15 weeks, test people with risk factors (and consider testing everyone) for undiagnosed diabetes using standard non-pregnant criteria; screen all others for GDM at 24 to 28 weeks. The IADPSG and two-step criteria were not derived for early pregnancy and should not be used before 24 weeks.

Diabetes in pregnancy (WHO 2013), managed as pre-existing diabetes: fasting 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more, 2-hour 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more after 75 g glucose, or random 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or more with symptoms.

Early abnormal glucose metabolism (fasting 110 to 125 mg/dL (6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L) or HbA1c 5.9 to 6.4%) marks higher risk, but the benefit of treatment before 24 weeks is uncertain and about one third regress on repeat testing (ADA 2026). Offer nutrition counselling and periodic fasting glucose checks, and decide on early treatment with the woman.

NICE uses risk-factor testing: BMI 30 or more, previous baby 4.5 kg or more, previous GDM, a first-degree relative with diabetes, or a family origin with high diabetes prevalence (including South Asian). Offer these women a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks.
Previous GDM (NICE): self-monitoring or a 75 g OGTT as soon as possible after booking, and a repeat OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks if normal. Glycosuria of 2+ once or 1+ twice should prompt testing.

sections.title: Diagnostic criteria at 24 to 28 weeks
items: One-step (ADA preferred; WHO 2013 and IADPSG): 75 g OGTT in the morning after an overnight fast of at least 8 hours. GDM if any value is met or exceeded: fasting 92 mg/dL (5.1 mmol/L), 1-hour 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L), 2-hour 153 mg/dL (8.5 mmol/L).

Two-step (ADA alternative, ACOG): 50 g non-fasting load; if the 1-hour value is 130, 135 or 140 mg/dL (7.2, 7.5 or 7.8 mmol/L) or more, do a fasting 100 g OGTT. GDM if 2 or more values reach fasting 95, 1-hour 180, 2-hour 155, 3-hour 140 mg/dL (5.3, 10.0, 8.6, 7.8 mmol/L); ACOG accepts one.
NICE: 75 g 2-hour OGTT; GDM if fasting 101 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) or more, or 2-hour 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or more.
Criteria identify different women (the one-step test diagnoses more GDM); each service should use one approach consistently. Measure HbA1c at diagnosis to detect pre-existing type 2 diabetes (NICE).
NICE advises against using fasting or random glucose, HbA1c, a glucose challenge test or urinalysis to assess GDM risk; the diagnostic test is the OGTT.

sections.title: First line: nutrition, activity and monitoring
items: Refer to a dietitian: a pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains and lean protein with controlled carbohydrate, spread through the day; lifestyle change alone suffices for many women (ADA).
Advise regular exercise, for example walking for 30 minutes after a meal (NICE).
Teach self-monitoring of capillary glucose: fasting and 1-hour after meals daily (NICE); ADA advises fasting and postprandial checks.

Targets (ADA, not on insulin): fasting below 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L) and 1-hour below 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or 2-hour below 120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). NICE: fasting 95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L), 1-hour 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or 2-hour 115 mg/dL (6.4 mmol/L).
On insulin, ADA lower limits are fasting 70, 1-hour 110 and 2-hour 100 mg/dL (3.9, 6.1, 5.6 mmol/L); NICE keeps glucose above 72 mg/dL (4 mmol/L).
NICE: review in a joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week of diagnosis, then contact every 1 to 2 weeks. ADA: telehealth combined with in-person visits improves outcomes.

sections.title: Medication when targets are not met
items: ADA 2026: insulin is the preferred drug for GDM. Metformin and glyburide are not first line because they cross the placenta, long-term offspring data are limited, and they fail to achieve targets in about 23 to 28% of women. Sulfonylureas increase neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia.

NICE (differs): fasting glucose below 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) at diagnosis, trial of diet and exercise; if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks, offer metformin; offer insulin if metformin is unsuitable or declined, or add it if targets are still not met.

NICE: fasting glucose 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more at diagnosis, start insulin immediately (with or without metformin) plus lifestyle changes; fasting 108 to 124 mg/dL (6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L) with macrosomia or polyhydramnios, consider immediate insulin.

Insulin: basal NPH or glargine for fasting hyperglycaemia (detemir is no longer marketed), and rapid-acting aspart or lispro before meals for postprandial peaks. Individualise and titrate every few days to targets; rotate injection sites.
Hypoglycaemia (below 70 mg/dL, 3.9 mmol/L): 15 to 20 g of fast-acting glucose, recheck after 15 minutes, then a snack. Teach the woman and family, and advise on driving safety.
Diabetes is not a contraindication to antenatal corticosteroids for preterm birth; give extra insulin by an agreed protocol and monitor glucose closely (NICE). Avoid betamimetic tocolytics.

sections.title: Fetal monitoring and birth
items: Ultrasound of fetal growth and liquor volume every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks (NICE); routine fetal wellbeing tests before 38 weeks are not needed unless growth restriction is suspected.

Timing of birth (NICE): advise birth no later than 40 weeks plus 6 days in uncomplicated GDM, offering induction or caesarean section if needed; consider earlier birth for maternal or fetal complications.
For an ultrasound-diagnosed macrosomic fetus, discuss the risks and benefits of vaginal birth, induction and caesarean section.
In labour check capillary glucose hourly and keep it between 72 and 126 mg/dL (4 and 7 mmol/L); use IV dextrose and insulin if it is not maintained (NICE).

Baby: feed within 30 minutes of birth, then every 2 to 3 hours until pre-feed glucose is at least 36 mg/dL (2.0 mmol/L); use tube feeds or IV dextrose if glucose stays below this on 2 readings or the baby has clinical signs (NICE).

sections.title: After birth: long-term follow-up
items: Stop glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth and check glucose before transfer to community care to exclude persisting hyperglycaemia. Encourage breastfeeding, which lowers later type 2 diabetes risk.
ADA: 75 g OGTT at 4 to 12 weeks postpartum using non-pregnant criteria. NICE: fasting plasma glucose at 6 to 13 weeks (HbA1c if later than 13 weeks) and no routine OGTT.

NICE interpretation: fasting below 108 mg/dL (6.0 mmol/L) low probability; 108 to 124 mg/dL (6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L) high risk; 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more likely type 2 diabetes (confirm). HbA1c 39 to 47 mmol/mol (5.7 to 6.4%) high risk; 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more diabetes.
Lifelong screening: every 1 to 3 years (ADA) or annual HbA1c (NICE). Prediabetes with overweight or obesity: intensive lifestyle intervention and/or metformin (ADA).
Counsel about recurrence in future pregnancies and offer early testing or self-monitoring next time; plan contraception and preconception care.

sections.title: India and other settings
items: India: the MoHFW (DIPSI) pathway uses a single-step 75 g load regardless of fasting, diagnoses GDM at a 2-hour value of 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L) or more, and tests at first contact and again at 24 to 28 weeks. Follow the national pathway where it applies.
Where one-step or two-step OGTT is not feasible, NICE-style risk-based testing is an accepted alternative; do not use HbA1c alone.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Applying IADPSG or two-step criteria before 24 weeks, or missing overt diabetes in early pregnancy.
Diagnosing or following up GDM with HbA1c alone during pregnancy.
Using glyburide (glibenclamide), or continuing to intensify metformin when targets are not met instead of adding insulin.
Missing neonatal hypoglycaemia, or failing to arrange the postnatal glucose test and lifelong screening.

drugs.name: Insulin (NPH or glargine basal; aspart or lispro prandial)
drugs.dose: Individualised subcutaneous dosing guided by self-monitoring, titrated every 2 to 3 days to targets
drugs.notes: ADA first-line drug. Basal insulin for fasting hyperglycaemia, rapid-acting before meals for postprandial peaks. Stop after birth.

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally once or twice daily with meals, increased weekly to effect; usual maximum 2 to 2.5 g/day in divided doses
drugs.notes: NICE first drug if lifestyle fails for 1 to 2 weeks; ADA second line. Crosses the placenta; add insulin if targets are not met. Stop after birth.

drugs.name: Oral glucose (hypoglycaemia)
drugs.dose: 15 to 20 g fast-acting glucose orally; repeat if still below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) after 15 minutes, then a snack
drugs.notes: Women on insulin should carry glucose.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone (if preterm birth expected)
drugs.dose: 6 mg IM every 12 hours for 4 doses
drugs.notes: Not contraindicated in diabetes; expect hyperglycaemia for several days and increase insulin by protocol.
